summary: Defines a profile for using X.509 Attribute Certificates in Internet protocols. Attribute certificates bind attributes such as roles or permissions to a holder, and may be used for authorization across a range of environments. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: An ID card shows who you are. An attribute certificate is like a badge that says what you are allowed to do. This document explains how to use those badges on the Internet.

subtitle: How to use X.509 attribute certificates to carry roles, groups and clearances, separate from a person's identity certificate.

tldr.problem: Authorization data such as group membership or clearance often has a different lifetime and a different authority than the identity-and-key binding in a public key certificate, so stuffing it into that certificate works poorly.
tldr.mechanism: The profile constrains the X.509 attribute certificate (AC): a signed structure with a holder, an issuer, a validity period and attributes but no public key. It fixes which fields, extensions, attribute types, validation rules and revocation schemes implementations must support.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3281, correcting errata and clarifying details, and gives generic applications a common baseline for ACs.

today: RFC 5755 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 3281, correcting errata and clarifying text, as listed in its Appendix D.

sections.title: Attribute Certificates and Why They Exist
sections.content:
An X.509 public key certificate (PKC) binds an identity to a public key. An attribute certificate (AC) is a similar structure with one main difference: it contains no public key. Instead it holds attributes that specify group membership, role, security clearance or other authorization information about the AC holder.

The RFC offers an analogy. A PKC is like a passport: it identifies the holder, lasts a long time and is not trivial to obtain. An AC is more like an entry visa: it is typically issued by a different authority and does not last as long. Getting a visa is simpler because you present a passport to get it.

Putting authorization data into a PKC extension is usually undesirable for two reasons. It often has a different lifetime from the identity binding, which shortens the PKC's useful life. And the PKC issuer is not usually authoritative for that information. An AC solves both by being a digitally signed identity plus a set of attributes. It can be used for access control, data origin authentication and non-repudiation, and is especially useful for role-based access control.
sections.eli5: Your school ID stays the same for years, but a hall pass changes every day. Putting the hall pass information on the ID would make a mess, so you carry a separate pass.

sections.title: Push, Pull and Delegation
sections.content:
The profile deals with the simple case in which one authority issues all of the ACs for a particular set of attributes. Chains of ACs used for delegation are complex, and the use of ACs on the Internet was quite limited, so implementations are RECOMMENDED not to use AC chains. Conforming implementations only have to process a single AC at a time, though several different authorities may each issue ACs for different attributes, such as a group in one and a clearance in another.

There are two ways to get an AC to a server. In the push model the client sends the AC to the server as part of the application protocol, so no new connection or search is needed and the verifier sees only what it needs to know. In the pull model the client just authenticates, and the server fetches the AC from the issuer or a repository, which can work without changing the client or the protocol. This profile does not specify a protocol for these exchanges.

The terminology is simple. The AC issuer (also called the Attribute Authority, AA) signs the AC. The AC holder is the entity named in the Holder field. The AC verifier checks the AC and uses the result.
sections.eli5: You can hand your pass to the guard yourself (push), or the guard can phone the office to check it (pull). Either way, one office signs the pass.

sections.title: The Profiled Fields
sections.content:
The AC is a signed structure whose main part, AttributeCertificateInfo, has these fields: version, holder, issuer, signature, serial number, validity period, attributes, an optional issuer unique identifier and optional extensions. The profile tightens each of them so different implementations interoperate.

  • Version MUST be v2.
  • Holder can name the holder by baseCertificateID (the issuer and serial number of the holder's PKC), by entityName, or by objectDigestInfo. The RFC RECOMMENDS using only one option per AC, and says the Holder field SHOULD use baseCertificateID when authentication is based on a PKC.
  • Issuer MUST use the v2Form with exactly one name, a non-empty distinguished name, so all AC issuers need such a name.
  • Serial number together with the issuer MUST be unique, MUST be positive, and MUST NOT be longer than 20 octets. Users must handle values longer than 4 octets.
  • Validity period uses GeneralizedTime in UTC with seconds and no fractions. Users MUST handle ACs whose validity is in the past or future, for example for backup.
  • Attributes MUST contain at least one attribute, and each attribute type may occur only once per AC, though it can have several values.
sections.eli5: The badge has a fixed layout: who it is for, who signed it, when it starts and stops, a unique number, and what it lets you do. The rules make sure every badge is laid out the same way.

sections.title: Extensions
sections.content:
Extensions describe the AC itself rather than the holder. A system MUST reject an AC that has a critical extension it does not recognize, while an unrecognized non-critical extension may be ignored. The profile defines these:

  • Audit identity (must be critical, 1 to 20 octets) is an opaque value so audit trails can follow a holder without identifying them. The issuer must be able to map it back to the real identity if misbehavior is detected.
  • AC targeting (must be critical) lists the servers or groups where the AC may be used. An honest verifier that is not a target MUST reject the AC. Without the extension, any server may accept it.
  • Authority key identifier (must not be critical) helps check the signature and SHOULD be included.
  • Authority information access (must not be critical) can point to an OCSP responder through an HTTP URL.
  • CRL distribution points (must not be critical) allow exactly one distribution point, with an HTTP or LDAP URL.
  • No revocation available (must not be critical) states that no revocation information will ever be published for this AC.
sections.eli5: Extensions are notes stamped on the badge: this badge only works at the library, or nobody can cancel this badge early. If the guard sees a must-obey note they cannot read, they refuse the badge.

sections.title: Standard Attribute Types
sections.content:
The profile defines six standard attribute types, so different issuers' ACs can be read the same way. Several use IetfAttrSyntax, which allows a separate policy authority and restricts values to an octet string, an object identifier or a UTF-8 string, all of one choice within an attribute.

  • Service authentication information identifies the holder to a service by name and can carry service-specific authentication data, typically a username and password for a legacy application. It is usually encrypted in that case.
  • Access identity identifies the holder so the verifier can authorize the holder's actions. Its authInfo field MUST NOT be present.
  • Charging identity says who to charge, for example the holder's company.
  • Group carries group memberships.
  • Role carries role allocations, with an optional role authority so that an administrator role from one organization can be told apart from another's. The role name MUST be a URI.
  • Clearance carries a security clearance. The basic hierarchy, in ascending order, is unmarked, unclassified, restricted, confidential, secret and top-secret. Implementations MUST NOT output the erroneous clearance syntax from RFC 3281.
sections.eli5: A badge can say your name for the front desk, who pays for you, which team you are on, your job, and how secret a room you may enter.

sections.title: Validation and Revocation
sections.content:
An AC is valid only if all of these hold. If the holder authenticates with a PKC, that PKC and its certification path are verified. The AC signature is correct, and the issuer's PKC path is verified and conforms to the profile. The issuer is directly trusted as an AC issuer. The evaluation time is within the validity period (equal to either end counts). The targeting check passes. And there is no unsupported critical extension. The issuer's own PKC must not belong to a CA, so an AC issuer cannot also be a PKC issuer, to avoid confusion over serial numbers and revocation.

Revocation has two schemes. Short-lived ACs, measured in hours, often need none because they expire before revocation data could spread. In the never revoke scheme the AC carries the noRevAvail extension, and verifiers MUST support it. In the pointer in AC scheme the AC points to revocation sources using authority information access or CRL distribution points, and verifiers SHOULD support it. An AC MUST NOT contain both. An AC without noRevAvail implicitly promises that some revocation method exists.
sections.eli5: The guard checks that the badge is real, signed by someone they trust, not expired, meant for this building, and has no secret instructions they cannot read. Some badges say cannot be cancelled, and others say call this number to check.

sections.title: Optional Features
sections.content:
Conformance does not require these features, but when they are offered they MUST work as described.

Attribute encryption keeps sensitive attributes private when an AC travels in the clear. Attributes are encrypted for chosen recipients using the CMS EnvelopedData structure before the AC is signed and are carried in an encAttrs attribute. The cleartext includes the issuer and serial number, which the verifier MUST check after decryption to stop ciphertext being copied from another AC. If an AC has attributes apparently encrypted for the verifier and decryption fails, the AC MUST be rejected.

Proxying lets a server act as a client for the holder, under the issuer's control, using a critical ProxyInfo extension that lists sets of permitted targets. ObjectDigestInfo links an AC to a hash of a public key or a whole PKC rather than to a name; the other object type MUST NOT be used. AA controls is a PKC extension that says which attribute types an AC issuer may include, through permitted and excluded lists and a flag for unspecified types.
sections.eli5: You can put a secret in a sealed envelope inside the badge, say which guards may pass it along, tie it to a fingerprint instead of a name, or limit what kinds of badge an office may print.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main risk is the AC issuer's private key. If it is stolen, an attacker can create false ACs or false revocation status, and if compromise is detected all ACs from that issuer MUST be revoked. Losing the key is also a problem, because the issuer could not renew ACs or produce revocation status, so secure backups are advised. Weak keys or hash algorithms limit how far an AC can be trusted, and untimely revocation status lowers confidence in long-lived ACs.

Name handling is another risk. Inconsistent name comparison can lead to accepting invalid targeted or proxied ACs. Issuers MUST encode the distinguished name in the holder's entityName identically to the holder's PKC. If an AC is tied by baseCertificateID and a rogue CA uses the same issuer name, it could issue a PKC with the same serial number to a malicious party. The RFC says to avoid duplicate CA names, or tie the AC to the PKC with a digest.

Verifiers MUST use only attributes that the issuer is trusted to issue, ignoring the rest, which matters most when more than one AC issuer is trusted. When the holder is authenticated without a PKC, the mapping from authenticated identity to AC holder is weaker and implementers SHOULD be very careful.
sections.eli5: If someone steals the office's stamp, they can print fake badges, so guard the stamp. Also make sure the name on the badge really matches the person at the door.
